messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dennis Alvarez was 68 years old, married, and still working part-time as a school counselor, but the assault that had happened years earlier continued to organize his days in ways that felt both humiliating and unavoidable. He had been walking back to his car after a late community meeting when two men crowded him near a strip of storefronts, one of them reeking of alcohol, the other shoving him hard enough that the pavement seemed to lurch upward. Dennis remembered it not as a continuous scene but as a handful of pictures: the glare of a parking lot light, a fist driving toward his face, the slick edge of a curb under his shoulder, the sour wash of beer on a stranger’s breath. When he tried to think about it, the same terror rushed back through him as if he were there again, trapped in those few frozen moments, and even now fragments of the memory could break loose without warning and vanish just as quickly, leaving him shaken and disoriented.

Over time, certain ordinary experiences began to hook directly into that memory. The smell of antiseptic in the hospital where he later went for treatment after the assault could hit him in a hallway or examination room and instantly call up the panic of being pinned helpless on the ground. Alcohol smell had the same effect; a passing whiff from someone in a grocery store or at a family gathering could pull him back into the fear of that night. He noticed, too, that when someone started getting emotionally close to him, the old helplessness returned in a different form. Intimacy made him feel exposed, as though closeness itself could become a way of being overpowered, and that sense of threat sharpened the memory until it felt immediate again.

In the months that followed, Dennis began managing those reactions by trying to leave his body whenever the fear rose too sharply. He would deliberately go blank, stare through people, or focus so hard on the pattern of tiles or the pressure of his feet that he could make himself feel far away. He avoided other people whenever he could, taking lunch alone in his office at school and finding reasons not to linger after meetings. With his wife, who had always been affectionate and emotionally open, he pulled back from intimacy and kept conversations practical, because being emotionally close felt like standing too near the edge of that old danger. He had come to believe that if he stayed distant enough, no one would get close enough to hurt him.

But those efforts brought their own costs. The more he kept away from people, the less practiced he felt in being around them, and the more startling it became when a student’s parent leaned in with the faint smell of alcohol on his clothes or when the disinfectant odor from the school nurse’s office drifted into the counseling suite. His deliberate blanking out helped for a moment, yet it also left him feeling less grounded, more vulnerable to sudden pieces of the assault surfacing in the middle of a workday. Each time that happened, he became more determined to avoid situations that might stir it up again, including closeness with his wife, whose concern he could feel but could not bear to meet directly. In that way, the fear kept circling back: the memory intensified his attempts to shut down and withdraw, and those very habits made the smells, the fleeting emotional closeness, and the sudden fragments easier to encounter and harder to tolerate. At school he still functioned, but he was increasingly tense in meetings, guarded with colleagues, and preoccupied with finding exits, as if any ordinary interaction could unexpectedly turn threatening.

By the time he sought help, Dennis was exhausted by the narrowness of his life and troubled by how alone he felt in his own marriage. What finally brought him in was realizing that he had begun to dread the school nurse’s hallway and even family dinners if there was wine on the table, and that he was pushing away the very people he most wanted to stay connected to. He hoped therapy might help him stay present when the terror surged and stop living as though every approach, every smell, and every moment of closeness might become the assault all over again.
